title.en: The Dice Game: The Pandawa Lose Everything
title.zh: 擲骰之局：般度五子盡失所有

region.zh: 哈斯提那（爪哇哇揚戲地理）

texts.period: Wayang purwa tradition; Old Javanese Mahabharata adaptations (Worsfold 1893)

source.work: W. Basil Worsfold, A Visit to Java (1893), chs. XII-XIV (the wayang cycle); Javanese Mahabharata tradition

summary.en: Summoned to Hastina, the eldest Pandawa, Puntadewa (Yudistira), is drawn into the loaded dice game: kingdom, brothers, himself, and finally Drupadi are staked and lost. The five brothers and their wife are sent into twelve years of forest exile with one final year to be passed in disguise — the wayang's grand scene of royal ruin by crooked chance.
summary.zh: 般度長子堅戰（蓬圖德瓦）應召赴哈斯提那，落入作弊骰局：王國、兄弟、自身乃至黑公主德羅帕迪逐一押上，盡數輸卻。五兄弟與妻被迫十二年林居流放，末年更須匿姓埋名——哇揚戲以此為『巧詐之運傾覆王室』之大場面。

sensitivity.note: Javanese Mahabharata (wayang purwa) paraphrase; the dice game is a fixed wayang lakon (play).

passages.text: The Kurawa cousins invite Puntadewa to the game of dice played with the enchanted bones; kingdom after kingdom, his brothers' freedom, his own, and at last Drupadi are staked and lost against a cheat's certainty.
passages.note: Paraphrase of the Javanese Mahabharata tradition (wayang purwa) as described in Worsfold (1893); not verbatim.

passages.text: The five Pandawa and Drupadi are banished to the forest for twelve years, with a thirteenth year to be lived in disguise; if they are discovered in that year, the exile begins again — the condition that will drive the last year's courtship of servitude in the enemy's city.
passages.note: Paraphrase of the Javanese Mahabharata tradition; not verbatim.

texts.period: Wayang purwa tradition; Javanese Mahabharata adaptations (Worsfold 1893)

source.work: W. Basil Worsfold, A Visit to Java (1893); Javanese Mahabharata tradition

summary.en: Dragged into the hall after being staked at dice, Drupadi is ordered disrobed before the assembled princes; Dursasana winds her garment round his hand and pulls — and the cloth never ends, yards upon yards flowing from her body until the hall is heaped with cloth and the molester falls exhausted. The wayang's miracle of the endless sash is the war's moral warrant.
summary.zh: 德羅帕迪被押入大殿，命其當眾去衣；難降以衣纏手用力拉扯——衣卻永無盡頭，一匹又一匹自其身湧出，堆積滿殿，行惡者力竭而倒。哇揚戲之『無盡衣』神蹟，為大戰立下道德之據。

sensitivity.note: Dignity-restoration miracle; paraphrased with care regarding the violence it responds to.

passages.text: Won at dice and dragged by the hair into the hall, Drupadi defies the Kurawa princes; Dursasana is ordered to disrobe her, and winds her sash around his hand to pull it from her body.
passages.note: Paraphrase of the Javanese Mahabharata tradition (wayang purwa); not verbatim.

passages.text: The cloth never ends: yard after yard unwinds until the hall is heaped high and Dursasana falls back exhausted. The Pandawa brothers raise their bound fists in oath, and Bima vows to drink the blood of the man who laid hands on her — the war of Kurushetra is here given its first warrant.
passages.note: Paraphrase of the Javanese Mahabharata tradition; not verbatim.

title.en: Karna: The Son of the Sun Set Adrift in a Basket
title.zh: 迦爾納：順流而下的太陽之子

texts.period: Wayang purwa tradition; Javanese Mahabharata adaptations

source.work: W. Basil Worsfold, A Visit to Java (1893); Javanese Mahabharata tradition

summary.en: Before her marriage, the princess Kunti tests a boon granted by the ascetic Durjasa and conceives by the god Batara Surya; fearing disgrace, she sets the child — born with golden ear-rings and impenetrable skin — adrift in the river. A charioteer's wife draws the basket up and raises the foundling as Karna, the sharpest archer of his generation, fated to fight on the wrong side of the war that will find him out.
summary.zh: 婚前，貢蒂試仙人達爾迦沙所賜之恩，感太陽神巴塔拉·蘇利亞而孕；懼失貞之名，將生有金耳環、金剛不壞之皮的新生兒置於木箱，順流而棄。御者之妻拾箱育之，是為迦爾納——當世第一神射手，命中注定為錯誤一方的戰爭而戰，直至身世被揭露。

sensitivity.note: Divine-foundling motif in the Javanese Mahabharata; paraphrased via wayang scholarship.

passages.text: Kunti, holding the boon that any god she calls will father her child, tests it in innocence and calls the sun; Batara Surya comes to her, and she bears a son armoured in golden skin with ear-rings fixed at birth.
passages.note: Paraphrase of the Javanese Mahabharata tradition (wayang purwa); not verbatim.

passages.text: To save her name she sets the child adrift in a basket on the river; a charioteer's household draws him up and names him Karna. His archery is unmatched — but his birth is a secret that the war will one day drag into the open.
passages.note: Paraphrase of the Javanese Mahabharata tradition; not verbatim.

title.en: Karna Refuses: 'The Charioteer's Son Chooses His Friends'
title.zh: 迦爾納之拒：『御者之子自擇其友』

texts.period: Wayang purwa tradition; Javanese Mahabharata adaptations

source.work: W. Basil Worsfold, A Visit to Java (1893); Javanese Mahabharata tradition

summary.en: On the eve of battle Kunti finds Karna at the river and offers to make him a Pandawa; Karna answers that the charioteer's wife who raised him is his mother, and the friend who made him a raja is his family — he will fight for Duryodana. He grants her only that of her five sons she shall keep at least one alive, and keeps her secret.
summary.zh: 大戰前夕，貢蒂於河畔尋得迦爾納，許以般度子之名分；迦爾納答曰：養我之御者妻即是吾母，賜我王位之友即是吾族——吾必為難敵而戰。唯允諾：五子之中，至少留一子性命。並守其母之密而不宣。

sensitivity.note: Loyalty-over-birth episode; a wayang favourite (Karna Tanding).

passages.text: Kunti comes to Karna on the eve of the war and offers to reveal him as the eldest Pandawa; Karna refuses: the woman who drew him from the river is his mother, the king who crowned him is his brother, and he will not trade their faith for birthright.
passages.note: Paraphrase of the Javanese Mahabharata tradition (wayang purwa); not verbatim.

passages.text: He asks her only to keep the secret until the war is done, and promises that of her five sons he will leave her at least one alive — then keeps her secret to his death, fighting the brothers he might have commanded.
passages.note: Paraphrase of the Javanese Mahabharata tradition; not verbatim.

texts.period: Wayang purwa tradition; Javanese Mahabharata adaptations (Worsfold 1893)

source.work: W. Basil Worsfold, A Visit to Java (1893); Javanese Mahabharata tradition

summary.en: Born of Bima and the giantess Arimbi, the infant Gatotkaca is so strong that his grandfather rages at the omen and hurls the baby into the sky; the child falls to earth from the clouds and the ground does not break under him — an established wayang icon. Trained in the sky, he becomes the flying warrior with the iron pancreas (maja pait) and the wired bones (wisnu janma? the kitang antaka) — the Pandawa's air force.
summary.zh: 五子怖軍與巨人族雅林比所生之嬰戈陀卡查，天生神力；其外祖父怒此異兆，將嬰孩擲向天空——嬰兒自雲霄墜地而大地不裂（哇揚戲定式）。後於天界受訓，成為『苦楝入骨』『 wired bones』之飛行戰士——般度軍之空軍。

sensitivity.note: Javanese wayang innovation: Gatotkaca's sky-birth and sky-training are distinctively Javanese, not in the Indian epic.

passages.text: The infant son of Bima and the giantess Arimbi shows strength beyond mortal measure; in fury and wonder the giant kindred hurl him toward the sky, and he falls back from the clouds to the earth without breaking the ground.
passages.note: Paraphrase of the Javanese Mahabharata tradition (wayang purwa); not verbatim.

passages.text: Taken up and trained in the heavens, he returns as the flying knight Gatotkaca — invulnerable to all weapons of earth by the iron bone within him — and becomes the terror of the Kurawa's chariots when he takes the air.
passages.note: Paraphrase of the Javanese Mahabharata tradition; not verbatim.

texts.period: Bharatayuddha kakawin, composed c. 1157 CE at Kediri (Sedah and Suralaya)

source.work: Kakawin Bharata Yuddha (c. 1157 CE), the death of Gatotkaca; Javanese war narrative

summary.en: Karna has but one arrow that can kill a flying god-ward: the Kuntawijayadanu, held in reserve by Krishna's counsel against the day it is aimed at Arjuna. Gatotkaca's night assault on the Kurawa camp forces Karna's hand — the arrow flies, the flying knight falls, and the Pandawa lose the terror of the skies while Karna loses the shot that was kept for Arjuna.
summary.zh: 迦爾納只有一支能殺飛行之神的箭——『恭塔維賈亞』；依克裏希那之策，此箭本為射阿周那而留。戈陀卡查夜襲俱盧大營，逼得迦爾納不得不放箭——飛騎殞落，般度軍失去空中之威；而迦爾納失去那支本為阿周那而留之箭。

sensitivity.note: Kakawin war episode; the strategic sacrifice is read in Java as Kresna's chess.

passages.text: Karna holds in reserve the one weapon that can bring down the invulnerable flying warrior; Kresna has warned the Pandawa that the arrow is aimed at Arjuna. On the night the Kurawa camp is broken, Gatotkaca's assault forces Karna to spend the shot on him.
passages.note: Paraphrase of the Bharatayuddha kakawin (c. 1157) narrative; not verbatim.

passages.text: The arrow flies, the iron-boned knight falls from the sky, and the Pandawa mourn their air-lord while counting the exchange a victory: Karna has fired his certain death, and the bowman who might have killed Arjuna has spent it on the giant's son.
passages.note: Paraphrase of the Bharatayuddha kakawin narrative; not verbatim.

title.en: The Bharatayuddha of Kediri: Kurushetra on Javanese Soil
title.zh: 諫義里《婆羅多之戰》：爪哇大地上的俱盧之野

region.zh: 東爪哇諫義里（創作宮廷）

texts.period: Composed c. 1157 CE (kakawin by Mpu Sedah and Mpu Suralaya) for the court of Kediri

source.work: Kakawin Bharata Yuddha (c. 1157 CE), court epic of Kediri

summary.en: Java's greatest war-poem retells the Mahabharata's climactic war in courtly kakawin verse, composed by two rival court poets (Mpu Sedah and Mpu Suralaya) for King Jayabaya of Kediri — in Javanese tradition, a king famed for prophecy. The poem's eighteen-day war is read as an allegory for the politics of its own century, and as the charter of the wayang war-plays.
summary.zh: 爪哇最偉大之戰詩以宮廷頌詩重述《摩訶婆羅多》決戰，由諫義里王查亞巴雅（爪哇傳統中的預言之王）之兩位御用詩人賽達與蘇拉拉雅合著。詩中十八日大戰被讀作其世紀政治之寓言，亦為哇揚戰戲之憲章。

sensitivity.note: Court epic; the Jayabaya prophecy-legend attaches to this poem's royal patron.

passages.text: The court poets of Kediri compose the war of the Pandawa and Kurawa in kakawin verse — the rival masters Sedah and Suralaya dividing the cantos — for a king whose court read the Indian war as the mirror of its own politics.
passages.note: Paraphrase of the Bharatayuddha kakawin (c. 1157) and its composition-legend; not verbatim.

passages.text: In the poem the eighteen days of Kurushetra are fought in Javanese terms — Kresna as the charioteer-god, Gatotkaca in the sky, Bima's mace, Karna's arrow — and the great lines of the Javanese war-poetry descend from it into the wayang repertoire.
passages.note: Paraphrase of the Bharatayuddha kakawin's reception; not verbatim.

title.en: Bima Breaks the Thigh of Duryodana

source.work: Kakawin Bharata Yuddha (c. 1157 CE); final mace-duel episode

summary.en: The war closes with the mace-duel of Bima and Duryodana. Forbidden by the rules of combat to strike below the navel, Bima waits until Kresna — drumming his own thigh as a signal — reminds him of the insult to Drupadi; the mace comes down on the thigh, the usurper's pride is broken with his bone, and the eighteen days end.
summary.zh: 大戰終結於怖軍與難敵之鐵杵決鬥。鬥規禁止擊腰以下；克裏希那拍擊己股示意——怖軍憶起德羅帕迪之辱，鐵杵落下，股骨碎裂，篡位者之傲與其骨同碎；十八日之戰遂終。

sensitivity.note: Breaking the combat taboo to end the war — flagged as interpretive in the Javanese retellings, where Kresna's signal is explicit.

passages.text: In the last duel the maces of Bima and Duryodana break against each other while the hosts stand down; the rules of the fight forbid a blow below the navel, and Bima's fury is checked by the law.
passages.note: Paraphrase of the Bharatayuddha kakawin (c. 1157); not verbatim.

passages.text: Kresna drums his hand upon his own thigh; Bima, reading the signal and remembering Drupadi, swings the mace down upon the thigh of Duryodana. The bone of the usurper breaks with his pride, and the war of the eighteen days is over.
passages.note: Paraphrase of the Bharatayuddha kakawin; not verbatim.

title.en: Abhimanyu in the Enclosure of Death

source.work: Kakawin Bharata Yuddha (c. 1157 CE); chakravyuha episode

summary.en: Abhimanyu, Arjuna's son, learned the breaking of the discus-formation in his mother's womb — but only the way in. At Kurushetra he pierces the wheel-array alone, fights through its concentric traps, and is killed inside it by a conspiracy of six; the wayang lakon of Abimanyu's death is the Javanese school of the young hero destroyed by knowledge half-given.
summary.zh: 阿周那之子激昂於母腹中習得破『轉輪陣』之法——惟知入而不知出。俱盧戰場上，他隻身突入輪陣，力破層層羅網，終為六人之合謀困殺於陣中。哇揚戲『激昂之死』即爪哇之堂課：僅授一半知識，足以毀掉年輕英雄。

sensitivity.note: Half-knowledge motif; the Javanese lakon stresses the mother's tale overheard in the womb.

passages.text: Abhimanyu learned the art of entering the discus-array while still unborn, listening as Kresna explained the formation to Subhadra; the explanation stopped at the way in, and the boy in the womb never heard the way out.
passages.note: Paraphrase of the Bharatayuddha kakawin (c. 1157) narrative; not verbatim.

passages.text: At Kurushetra the wheel-array closes around the young prince; he fights inward through the rings of the trap, but having no key to the exit he falls inside it, cut down by six champions together — the death that shames the war's law and hardens the Pandawa's heart.
passages.note: Paraphrase of the Bharatayuddha kakawin; not verbatim.

title.en: Kresna the Charioteer: The God Who Drives the War
title.zh: 禦者克裏希那：駕馭戰爭之神

source.work: Kakawin Bharata Yuddha (c. 1157 CE); Kresna's counsel and chariot

summary.en: In the Javanese war, the god Batara Kresna refuses armies and offers instead to drive Arjuna's chariot; from the box-seat between the two hosts he steers the whole battle — counselling, withholding and revealing weapons, arranging that Gatotkaca draws Karna's reserved arrow — the wayang's charioteer is the intelligence of the war wearing a mortal's seat.
summary.zh: 爪哇戰事之中，巴塔拉·克裏希那拒受兵馬，只求為阿周那禦車；於兩軍之間的車轅上，他駕馭全局——進策、藏箭、示箭，安排戈陀卡查誘出迦爾納之留箭。哇揚戲之禦者，乃坐在凡人座位上的戰爭智囊。

sensitivity.note: Kresna's warcraft; paraphrase of the kakawin's divine strategist.

passages.text: Asked to choose between the hosts, Kresna offers his person unarmed and his chariot without armies; the Pandawa take the god as charioteer, and the Kurawa take his troops.
passages.note: Paraphrase of the Bharatayuddha kakawin (c. 1157); not verbatim.

passages.text: From the driver's seat the god steers the eighteen days: he signals the thigh to Bima, holds Arjuna's bow steady at the moment of doubt, and disposes the death of Gatotkaca so that Karna's reserved arrow is spent — the war is won in the seat of the driver.
passages.note: Paraphrase of the Bharatayuddha kakawin; not verbatim.

title.en: Semar Sent Down to the Pandawa
title.zh: 塞馬爾下凡隨般度五子

texts.period: Wayang purwa tradition (Javanese innovation; Worsfold 1893 records the Punakawan)

source.work: W. Basil Worsfold, A Visit to Java (1893), the Punakawan servants of the wayang; Javanese wayang purwa tradition

summary.en: A purely Javanese invention: the gods send down Semar — pot-bellied, ironical, servile in speech — to serve the heroes as Punakawan clown-servant, with his sons Gareng, Petruk and Bagong. In the dalang's theology Semar outranks every god on the stage: the clown who carries the truth of the play, the deity who hides as a servant.
summary.zh: 純爪哇之創造：諸神遣塞馬爾——大腹便便、言語譏誚、口稱卑賤——攜三子加楞、佩特魯克、巴貢下凡，充當英雄之僕（普納卡萬丑角）。在達朗（戲偶師）的神學裏，塞馬爾位在臺上諸神之上：丑角承載戲之真理，神明隱於僕身。

sensitivity.note: Living wayang tradition; the Punakawan are a Javanese (not Indian) layer of the Mahabharata on Java.

passages.text: To keep the heroes of the plays human, the Javanese wayang adds what the Indian epic does not have: the Punakawan, clown-servants led by Semar, who fetch, advise, mock and out-think their masters between the battles.
passages.note: Paraphrase of the wayang purwa tradition as described in Worsfold (1893); not verbatim.

passages.text: Court theology makes the joke serious: the pot-bellied servant Semar is the oldest of the gods in disguise, granted to the Pandawa as companion and conscience. When the heroes listen to Semar they are listening, the dalang says, to the one voice on the stage above the gods.
passages.note: Paraphrase of the wayang purwa tradition; not verbatim.

title.en: The Pandawa Walk Away: The Great Renunciation

region.zh: 喜馬拉雅登天之路（哇揚戲結局）

texts.period: Wayang purwa tradition; Javanese Mahabharata adaptations

source.work: W. Basil Worsfold, A Visit to Java (1893); Javanese Mahabharata tradition

summary.en: The Mahabharata's Javanese finale: the Pandawa crown their heir, set aside their weapons, and walk toward the mountain of the gods in wedding garments — one by one they fall on the way as their secret failings are named, until Puntadewa alone, and the faithful dog, reaches the summit.
summary.zh: 爪哇版《摩訶婆羅多》之終章：般度五子立嗣君，卸下武器，著婚衣向諸神之山而行——旅途中他們的隱秘罪愆被逐一點名，逐一倒下；最後唯堅戰與那忠犬抵達山巔。

sensitivity.note: Renunciation-and-ascent finale; cross-cluster with Arda Viraf and other ascent narratives.

passages.text: After the war the Pandawa set their heir on the throne and begin the walk to heaven in royal garments; on the climb each falls in turn as the weight of an old failure is spoken aloud — the teller of lies, the glutton of pride, the keeper of a favour half-earned.
passages.note: Paraphrase of the Javanese Mahabharata tradition (wayang purwa); not verbatim.

passages.text: Puntadewa alone goes on, refusing at the gate of heaven to enter without the dog that has followed him; the dog is his own honour in disguise, and both are admitted — the wayang closes the epic on the reward of one flawless virtue.
passages.note: Paraphrase of the Javanese Mahabharata tradition; not verbatim.
